fatal_errors: The as-deposited material is incorrectly described as nanocrystalline, hexagonal, and already undergoing a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition; the target films and ribbons were amorphous or extremely fine/disordered with only cubic-type short-range order.

The proposed annealing mediator is grain growth and reduced grain-boundary density, whereas 700 K annealing produced no detectable crystallization, grain growth, phase decomposition, or major roughness change.
The mechanism centers on propagation and hysteresis of a magnetostructural phase transition that was not the governing behavior of the as-deposited thin-film system.

The predicted reduction of transition hysteresis and transition broadening does not reconstruct the observed increase in magnetization and modest entropy-change enhancement caused by short-range reordering and internal-strain relaxation.
No prior observations or citations are supplied to support the asserted nanocrystalline baseline or grain-boundary mechanism.
explanation: The response identifies post-deposition annealing as a potentially useful controlled intervention and proposes a reasonable annealed-versus-unannealed comparison using microscopy and magnetic measurements. However, its central structural premise is incompatible with the target system. The target samples remain amorphous/disordered after 700 K annealing, so grain growth cannot mediate the observed response. The supported explanation instead involves short-range atomic reordering, relaxation of fabrication-induced strain, reduced local pinning barriers, improved collective exchange, and a larger effective ferromagnetic fraction. The response also omits the key geometry and elastic-strain controls, the 700 K pre-crystallization boundary, the broad 40–200 K conventional response with an inverse effect below 20 K, and the measured entropy-change increase from about 1.25 to 1.35 J kg−1 K−1 at 140 K and 50 kOe. Its experiment could test its own grain-growth hypothesis, but the falsification rule is weakened because failure to produce grain growth would test the treatment rather than cleanly distinguish grain-boundary control from short-range relaxation.
